To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

sperm with fragmented-DNA are selected against during the sperm transport through the female genital tract and during ZP binding/penetration, and that the ability of the oocyte to prevent fertilization with spermatozoa bearing DNA damage depends on the source and the degree of damage.

spermatozoa are selected before fertilization by a preliminary mechanism that acts on sperm with low motility or fragmented-DNA, but this mechanism is not sufficient to prevent fertilization when spermatozoa have fragmented-DNA.
spermatozoa that are able to fertilize an oocyte must have a high motility and a low level of sperm-DNA fragmentation.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the selection of fertilization competent spermatozoa during the transport through female tract and/or during ZP binding/penetration.
the mechanisms of sperm selection in the oviduct.
a better understanding of the mechanisms of sperm-oviduct selection and the role of DNA damage in the process.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

in vivo fertilization is not only a process that involves sperm-oviduct and sperm-ZP interactions, but also a process of sperm selection that takes place in the utero-tubal junction, the uterus, and the oviduct and that involves the sperm DNA integrity.
the ZP is the main site of selection against sperm with fragmented DNA, but the selection mechanism depends on the origin of the DNA damage.
in postovulation mating there is a general selection against sperm with low motility but the ability of ZP to prevent penetration by fragmented-DNA is achieved only during the sperm-ZP penetration.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

spermatozoa are selected against during transport through the female genital tract, and during the spermatozoan interaction with the zona pellucid, and this selection is stronger for spermatozoa damaged by heat stress than by irradiation.
sperm with damaged DNA can fertilize the oocyte, but they are not able to develop to term.

in the mouse, DNA integrity is a key of sperm selection after postovulation mating, and the mechanism by which the ZP prevents fertilization by fragmented DNA spermatozoa depends on the type and source of the damage.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the ZP has an important role in the selection of fertilization-competent spermatozoa, and that this selection is dependent on the type of DNA damage.
DNA fragmentation in sperm is not always a negative factor for fertility.
sperm selection in postovulatory females is a complex process, and it is important to consider that different types of sperm damage may be treated differently.
